newsitem.title: GERMANY: Yeltsin banks on Kohl, aims for NATO treaty.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin banks on Kohl, aims for NATO treaty.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, apparently gambling on the support of his friend and ally Chancellor Helmut Kohl, said after talks in Germany on Thursday that Russia would clinch an elusive deal with NATO next month.

After a day of talks in the spa resort of Baden-Baden, home to the casino immortalised in Dostoevsky's 1860s Russian novel "The Gambler", Yeltsin and Kohl said German influence could break a deadlock between Moscow and the alliance over NATO's eastward expansion.

Yeltsin, looking pale and distracted, told reporters he and Kohl were in broad agreement on negotiations on a treaty intended to help to allay Russia's strong objections to NATO's planned inclusion of former Soviet states.

"We want to announce that...on the 27th of May in Paris an agreement will be signed by the leaders of the NATO countries and of Russia," he said, before making clear that much discussion remained by adding: "So we'll have to hurry."
Yeltsin said, peppering his comments with references to "my friend Helmut, said: "It was very important for me that Helmut Kohl supported Russia's line."

"I am sure that such an authoritative politician as Helmut Kohl will exert his influence so that there will be objectivity in these issues," he said, referring to Russia's demand that NATO must not advance nuclear and other weapons into its new members and for a say in NATO planning based on consensus decisions.

The meeting was the fifth between the two men since the start of last year and both were at pains to stress the warm friendship which has become an important tool in easing strain in relations between Russia and the West.
Kohl said he hoped a deal on NATO could be struck next month with German help. But he noted the obstacles ahead.
NATO leaders, especially the United States, are unwilling to conceded som nuch to Moscow that new members like Poland and Hungary would be consigned to "second-class" NATO participation.
"I am confident that, with goodwill on both sides, we can come to an agreement before the NATO-Russia summit on May 27," Kohl said.

But he noted that, while four chapters of the treaty were "90 percent" complete, a fifth, dealing with nuts and bolts military issues, posed significant problems. "It still needs a lot of work but I see good chances," he said.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said intense negotiations were now needed to make "realistic" the target of a May 27 signing in Paris agreed last week.

Yeltsin, 66 and back in action for only a couple of months after a long illness, looked tired but spoke clearly and smiled as he read a 15-minute speech in the evening accepting a "Man of the Year" award from the German media.

He said the award was a recognition of Russia's move to democracy and the end of the ideological conflict of the Cold War, a point that reinforced his objection to NATO's "alarming" plan to create new divisions in Europe.
Kohl and Yeltsin said they had also made progress in settling a long dispute over German art treasures seized by the Soviet Army after World War Two.

There would be no quick solution but in a gesture of goodwill Yeltsin brought Kohl a collection of papers of the 1922 German foreign minister Walther Rathenau and said he had ordered the release to Germany of copies of the East German communist party records held in Moscow since the 1970s.

Germany and Russia also aim to improve economic ties by setting up a new forum headed by both leaders and to promote Russia's membership of international economic organisations like the World Trade Organisation, the Group of Seven and the Paris Club of lenders.
Yeltsin and his wife Naina were to fly back to Russia on Friday morning, possibly direct to the Black Sea resort of Sochi where he is due to spend a few days holiday.
